scenario.name: IETF RFC 1035, Sysmon EID 22 & Unit 42 — Covert DNS Tunneling & Exfiltration DFIR
scenario.shortSubtitle: Network & Web · Subdomain Entropy, Recursive NS/TXT Beacons, Sysmon EID 22 & RPZ Sinkholing
scenario.overview: Imagine a walled coastal fortress where every outgoing cargo ship is blocked by a tall stone seawall. Trapped inside, a rogue clerk slices private harbor ledger sheets into tiny scrambled slips, ties each slip onto carrier pigeons disguised as routine harbor address inquiries, and sends them through the central postmaster tower straight out to an offshore lighthouse that flashes coded replies back, until the coastguard watchtower notices the impossibly gibberish scroll labels, traces which indoor desk is launching the pigeons, and drops an emerald harbor net over the rogue offshore island. In this scenario (T1071.004, Covert DNS Tunneling & Data Exfiltration) from WKSTN-FIN-14 through DNS-INT-01, a compromised endpoint smuggles staged files past web proxies along one continuous intrusion path using everyday DNS lookups. First, the implant slices stolen data into high-entropy hexadecimal subdomain labels attributed by Sysmon Event ID 22, then relays those unique uncached queries through the corporate recursive resolver to a rogue authoritative server returning TXT command replies, then triggers Zeek Shannon-entropy and Newly Observed Domain detection alerts, and finally gets severed by DNS Response Policy Zone sinkholing and outbound port 53/853 egress locks. Steps #1 through #4 trace each endpoint, resolver, and perimeter telemetry handoff, while the Memory Forensics section compares high-entropy tunnel query buffers against normal low-entropy enterprise DNS traffic.

stages.title: RFC 1035 Subdomain Chunking & Sysmon Event ID 22 Process Attribution
stages.subtitle: Encoding Stolen Data Into 63-Octet DNS Labels From an Isolated Endpoint
stages.description: At a dim desk inside the walled harbor, a rogue clerk cuts secret ledger pages into tiny equal-length scrambled paper strips small enough to fit inside carrier-pigeon leg capsules, unaware that a blue overhead skylight lens logs exactly which clerk’s desk launches every bird. Because IETF RFC 1035 (the foundational Internet specification defining how domain names are structured) caps every subdomain label at 63 characters and an entire domain name at 253 characters, DNS tunneling clients slice files into fixed-length encoded chunks (usually Hex or Base32 strings) prepended to an attacker-owned parent domain. On Windows endpoints, Microsoft Sysmon Event ID 22 (the kernel-assisted telemetry record capturing every DNS lookup together with the originating executable path and Process ID) immediately proves which specific binary generated those abnormal queries. On segmented workstation WKSTN-FIN-14 (10.10.44.14), outbound web proxies and direct HTTP/HTTPS connections are blocked, but standard internal DNS resolution remains open so corporate applications can function. Malicious binary C:\ProgramData\SyncCache\telemetry_sync.exe (PID 6248) reads staged finance files, encodes sequential 28-byte slices into 56-character hexadecimal labels, and calls DnsQuery_W(). Without Sysmon Event ID 22, network defenders only see queries arriving at DNS-INT-01 from WKSTN-FIN-14’s IP address without knowing which process emitted them. With Event ID 22 enabled, DFIR analysts immediately link the high-entropy lookup burst to an unsigned binary running out of C:\ProgramData\SyncCache. In the documented Sysmon EID 22 (DnsQuery) exchange from Isolated Backup Host (DB-BACKUP-02) to sync_agent.exe (DNS Exfil Agent), sync_agent.exe (DNS Exfil Agent) responds with ACK 56 Chars (confirming that the HEX SUBDOMAIN BURST request succeeded on sync_agent.exe (DNS Exfil Agent) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Recursive Resolver Forwarding to External Authoritative NS & TXT Replies). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ HEX SUBDOMAIN BURST / ⇠#1 ACK 56 Chars) from Node ③ (#3 Isolated Backup Host (DB-BACKUP-02)) to Node ④ (#4 sync_agent.exe (DNS Exfil Agent)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Zeek DNS NDR & Sysmon EID 22).

stages.title: Recursive Resolver Forwarding to External Authoritative NS & TXT Replies
stages.subtitle: Abusing Permitted Internal DNS Recursion as an Uncached Bidirectional Bridge
stages.description: Each carrier pigeon flies first to the trusted central harbor postmaster tower; because the postmaster has never seen those bizarre scrambled street names before, it dutifully relays every pigeon across the seawall to the rogue offshore lighthouse, which flashes coded lantern replies back. A DNS tunnel rarely needs direct Internet access from the compromised workstation: it leverages the organization’s own recursive DNS resolver (the internal server responsible for looking up external domain names on behalf of staff computers). Because every encoded subdomain string is unique and the attacker’s external authoritative name server (the Internet server officially designated to answer queries for that domain) returns TTL=0 (Time To Live of zero seconds, prohibiting caching), the internal resolver dutifully ferries data in both directions using outbound subdomain labels and inbound TXT or CNAME records. When DNS-INT-01 (10.10.2.53) receives a TXT lookup for 7e3d19a4c5b20f8e...s14.cdn-metrics-sync.example, it checks its local cache, finds no match, and resolves the NS delegation to 198.51.100.77:53. The attacker’s custom authoritative listener strips the leftmost label, stores the decoded sequence chunk, and sends back a TXT record with TTL=0.0 containing an acknowledgement or next encoded tasking block. Unit 42 documented this exact bidirectional TXT/A/AAAA relay architecture in OilRig (APT34) DNS tunneling families such as DNSpionage and BONDUPDATER, highlighting why internal resolvers must be monitored as high-priority perimeter egress points. In the documented Zeek dns.log (TXT · TTL=0) exchange from sync_agent.exe (DNS Exfil Agent) to Corp DNS Resolver & FW, Corp DNS Resolver & FW responds with RESP TTL=0.0 (confirming that the UNCACHED NS RELAY request succeeded on Corp DNS Resolver & FW and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Zeek Statistical Detection: Shannon Entropy > 4.2, Label Length & NOD Correlation). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ UNCACHED NS RELAY / ⇠#2 RESP TTL=0.0) from Node ④ (#4 sync_agent.exe (DNS Exfil Agent)) to Node ② (#2 Corp DNS Resolver & FW), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Zeek DNS NDR & Sysmon EID 22).

stages.title: Zeek Statistical Detection: Shannon Entropy > 4.2, Label Length & NOD Correlation
stages.subtitle: Why Mathematical DNS Telemetry Exposes Tunnels Regardless of Encoding Scheme
stages.description: High in the coastal watchtower, harbor analysts weigh the scrambled slips passing through the postmaster, realizing ordinary harbor addresses look like calm human words, whereas hundreds of random gibberish slips every minute bound for a four-day-old offshore island can only mean smuggling. Even if a threat actor switches between Hex, Base32, Base64, or custom ciphers, packing compressed or encrypted data into DNS labels creates unmistakable mathematical fingerprints: elevated Shannon entropy (a statistical measure of character randomness, typically > 4.0 bits/byte for encoded tunnels versus ~2.7–3.2 for normal hostnames), unusually long leftmost labels, near-100% cache-miss ratios, and high query counts targeting a Newly Observed Domain (a recently registered domain with zero prior enterprise history). Within 45 seconds of telemetry_sync.exe starting exfiltration, Zeek passive DNS telemetry and SIEM behavioral rules aggregate queries by registered apex domain (eTLD+1). While legitimate cloud CDNs occasionally generate high-entropy tokens, they rarely combine all five tunneling indicators simultaneously: 412 unique subdomains per minute, 56-character fixed leftmost labels, 4.41 bits/byte Shannon entropy, 78% TXT record type ratio with TTL=0, and a domain first observed only 4 days earlier. Correlating that Zeek alert with Sysmon Event ID 22 produces a zero-ambiguity P1 incident pinpointing both the exact exfiltrated volume (~184 KB) and the offending workstation process. In the documented SIEM Entropy & NOD Rule exchange from Corp DNS Resolver & FW to Attacker Authoritative DNS C2, Attacker Authoritative DNS C2 responds with ALERT 184 KB (confirming that the ENTROPY 4.41 SPIKE request succeeded on Attacker Authoritative DNS C2 and establishing the runtime state required for Step #4 DNS RPZ Sinkholing & Mandatory Internal Resolver Egress Enforcement). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ ENTROPY 4.41 SPIKE / ⇠#3 ALERT 184 KB) from Node ② (#2 Corp DNS Resolver & FW) to Node ① (#1 Attacker Authoritative DNS C2), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Zeek DNS NDR & Sysmon EID 22).

stages.title: DNS RPZ Sinkholing & Mandatory Internal Resolver Egress Enforcement
stages.subtitle: Breaking the Covert Channel in Milliseconds & Closing Direct Port 53/853 Bypasses
stages.description: Coastguard engineers drop a glowing emerald harbor net directly over the rogue offshore lighthouse so every coded inquiry lands harmlessly in the guardhouse, while sealing every unauthorized seawall gap so no pigeon can bypass the central postmaster. Effective DNS tunneling containment pairs two complementary controls: DNS Response Policy Zones (RPZ, often called a DNS firewall, allowing internal resolvers to block or redirect malicious domains to a controlled sinkhole IP in seconds) and strict perimeter egress filtering (blocking workstations from sending direct UDP/TCP port 53, DNS-over-TLS port 853, or unauthorized DNS-over-HTTPS traffic to external resolvers so every lookup must pass through inspected corporate servers). Upon confirming SIEM-ENTROPY-408, responders push a wildcard RPZ rule (*.cdn-metrics-sync.example -> sinkhole 10.255.255.53) to DNS-INT-01 and DNS-INT-02, instantly severing both outbound data exfiltration and inbound TXT command acknowledgements across the entire fleet. Simultaneously, network engineers verify that workstation VLAN firewalls enforce default-deny on outbound UDP/53, TCP/53, TCP/853 (DoT), and public DoH IP ranges, preventing malware from bypassing internal visibility. Finally, IR teams isolate WKSTN-FIN-14, capture volatile memory from telemetry_sync.exe (PID 6248), and reconstruct exfiltrated file scope from recorded query logs. On the diagram, follow Step #4 / Link #4 (#4→ RPZ SINKHOLE DROP / ⇠#4 RESP BLOCKED) from Node ② (#2 Corp DNS Resolver & FW) to Node ⑥ (#6 Zeek DNS NDR & Sysmon EID 22), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Zeek DNS NDR & Sysmon EID 22).

detectionRule.title: Non-Browser Process Generating High-Entropy Long DNS Queries (Sysmon EID 22)
detectionRule.ruleCode:
title: Suspicious Long Subdomain DNS Queries From Non-Browser Binary
status: stable
logsource:
  category: dns_query

detection:

detectionRule.title: Detect High-Volume Unique Subdomain DNS Tunneling by Apex Domain
detectionRule.ruleCode:
DnsEvents
| where QueryType in ("TXT", "CNAME", "NULL", "A")
| extend Apex = extract(@"([^\.]+\.[^\.]+)$", 1, Name), LeftLabel = tostring(split(Name, ".")[0])
| summarize UniqueQueries=dcount(Name), AvgLabelLen=avg(strlen(LeftLabel)) by ClientIP, Apex
| where UniqueQueries > 150 and AvgLabelLen > 38
detectionRule.mitigation: Correlate passive DNS entropy scoring with Newly Observed Domain (NOD) threat feeds and Sysmon Event ID 22 for zero-ambiguity P1 alerting.

Malicious binary C:\ProgramData\SyncCache\telemetry_sync.exe (PID 6248) reads staged finance files, encodes sequential 28-byte slices into 56-character hexadecimal labels, and calls DnsQuery_W(). Without Sysmon Event ID 22, network defenders only see queries arriving at DNS-INT-01 from WKSTN-FIN-14’s IP address without knowing which process emitted them. With Event ID 22 enabled, DFIR analysts immediately link the high-entropy lookup burst to an unsigned binary running out of C:\ProgramData\SyncCache.
steps.diagramAlignment: Follow Step #1 / Link #1 as Node 1 (WKSTN-FIN-14 PID 6248) encodes chunks and dispatches lookups toward Node 2 (DNS-INT-01) while Node 4 (Zeek + Sysmon 22) records process lineage.
steps.detectionAndEvidence: Enable Sysmon Event ID 22 across endpoints and hunt for non-browser binaries emitting high volumes of long, unique subdomain queries under a single apex domain.

steps.plainTitle: Recursive Resolver Forwarding to External Authoritative NS & TXT Replies
steps.storyAnalogy: Each carrier pigeon flies first to the trusted central harbor postmaster tower; because the postmaster has never seen those bizarre scrambled street names before, it dutifully relays every pigeon across the seawall to the rogue offshore lighthouse, which flashes coded lantern replies back.
steps.simpleExplanation: A DNS tunnel rarely needs direct Internet access from the compromised workstation: it leverages the organization’s own recursive DNS resolver (the internal server responsible for looking up external domain names on behalf of staff computers). Because every encoded subdomain string is unique and the attacker’s external authoritative name server (the Internet server officially designated to answer queries for that domain) returns TTL=0 (Time To Live of zero seconds, prohibiting caching), the internal resolver dutifully ferries data in both directions using outbound subdomain labels and inbound TXT or CNAME records.
steps.howItWorksInPractice: When DNS-INT-01 (10.10.2.53) receives a TXT lookup for 7e3d19a4c5b20f8e...s14.cdn-metrics-sync.example, it checks its local cache, finds no match, and resolves the NS delegation to 198.51.100.77:53. The attacker’s custom authoritative listener strips the leftmost label, stores the decoded sequence chunk, and sends back a TXT record with TTL=0.0 containing an acknowledgement or next encoded tasking block. Unit 42 documented this exact bidirectional TXT/A/AAAA relay architecture in OilRig (APT34) DNS tunneling families such as DNSpionage and BONDUPDATER, highlighting why internal resolvers must be monitored as high-priority perimeter egress points.
steps.diagramAlignment: Follow Step #2 / Link #2 as Node 2 (DNS-INT-01 Recursive) relays uncached lookups across the perimeter to Node 3 (Rogue Auth NS 198.51.100.77) and receives TTL=0 TXT replies.
steps.detectionAndEvidence: Monitor internal resolver forwarding logs (Zeek dns.log) for unusual spikes in TXT, NULL, or CNAME queries with TTL=0 directed at a single newly observed authoritative server.

steps.plainTitle: Zeek Statistical Detection: Shannon Entropy > 4.2, Label Length & NOD Correlation
steps.storyAnalogy: High in the coastal watchtower, harbor analysts weigh the scrambled slips passing through the postmaster, realizing ordinary harbor addresses look like calm human words, whereas hundreds of random gibberish slips every minute bound for a four-day-old offshore island can only mean smuggling.
steps.simpleExplanation: Even if a threat actor switches between Hex, Base32, Base64, or custom ciphers, packing compressed or encrypted data into DNS labels creates unmistakable mathematical fingerprints: elevated Shannon entropy (a statistical measure of character randomness, typically > 4.0 bits/byte for encoded tunnels versus ~2.7–3.2 for normal hostnames), unusually long leftmost labels, near-100% cache-miss ratios, and high query counts targeting a Newly Observed Domain (a recently registered domain with zero prior enterprise history).
steps.howItWorksInPractice: Within 45 seconds of telemetry_sync.exe starting exfiltration, Zeek passive DNS telemetry and SIEM behavioral rules aggregate queries by registered apex domain (eTLD+1). While legitimate cloud CDNs occasionally generate high-entropy tokens, they rarely combine all five tunneling indicators simultaneously: 412 unique subdomains per minute, 56-character fixed leftmost labels, 4.41 bits/byte Shannon entropy, 78% TXT record type ratio with TTL=0, and a domain first observed only 4 days earlier. Correlating that Zeek alert with Sysmon Event ID 22 produces a zero-ambiguity P1 incident pinpointing both the exact exfiltrated volume (~184 KB) and the offending workstation process.
steps.diagramAlignment: Follow Step #3 / Link #3 as Node 4 (Zeek + Sysmon 22) evaluates traffic between Node 2 (DNS-INT-01) and Node 3 (Rogue Auth NS) and raises SIEM-ENTROPY-408.
steps.detectionAndEvidence: Deploy Zeek dns.log / passive DNS scoring combining Shannon entropy (>= 3.9), unique subdomain ratio (> 0.85), TXT/CNAME frequency, and Newly Observed Domain age (< 30 days).

steps.plainTitle: DNS RPZ Sinkholing & Mandatory Internal Resolver Egress Enforcement
steps.storyAnalogy: Coastguard engineers drop a glowing emerald harbor net directly over the rogue offshore lighthouse so every coded inquiry lands harmlessly in the guardhouse, while sealing every unauthorized seawall gap so no pigeon can bypass the central postmaster.
steps.simpleExplanation: Effective DNS tunneling containment pairs two complementary controls: DNS Response Policy Zones (RPZ, often called a DNS firewall, allowing internal resolvers to block or redirect malicious domains to a controlled sinkhole IP in seconds) and strict perimeter egress filtering (blocking workstations from sending direct UDP/TCP port 53, DNS-over-TLS port 853, or unauthorized DNS-over-HTTPS traffic to external resolvers so every lookup must pass through inspected corporate servers).
steps.howItWorksInPractice: Upon confirming SIEM-ENTROPY-408, responders push a wildcard RPZ rule (*.cdn-metrics-sync.example -> sinkhole 10.255.255.53) to DNS-INT-01 and DNS-INT-02, instantly severing both outbound data exfiltration and inbound TXT command acknowledgements across the entire fleet. Simultaneously, network engineers verify that workstation VLAN firewalls enforce default-deny on outbound UDP/53, TCP/53, TCP/853 (DoT), and public DoH IP ranges, preventing malware from bypassing internal visibility. Finally, IR teams isolate WKSTN-FIN-14, capture volatile memory from telemetry_sync.exe (PID 6248), and reconstruct exfiltrated file scope from recorded query logs.
steps.diagramAlignment: Follow Step #4 / Link #4 as Node 5 (RPZ Sinkhole & FW Lock) seals DNS-INT-01 against Node 3 (Rogue Auth NS) while Node 4 confirms zero direct port 53/853 bypasses.
steps.detectionAndEvidence: Verify RPZ sinkhole hits drop to zero post-isolation, audit perimeter firewalls for blocked direct UDP/53/853 attempts, and preserve Zeek dns.log for data-loss reconstruction.
